newsitem.title: FRANCE: French Socialists could win in 1998 - poll.
newsitem.headline: French Socialists could win in 1998 - poll.

text.p: France's opposition Socialists could narrowly win next year's parliamentary elections if they manage to forge a pact with Communists and Greens, according to an opinion poll published on Wednesday.

"Less than a year from the normal date (March) for general elections, the game is open. That is the main lesson of the simulation in parliamentary seats," said the BVA survey for France 2 television and Paris-Match magazine.
It credited the Socialist Party with 28 percent of voting intentions and some 231 to 283 seats in parliament, out of a total of 555 metropolitan seats.
Communists and Greens are credited with 10.5 and nine percent of voting intentions respectively -- 20 to 25 seats for the former and two to six seats for the latter.
But the poll found that no group alone could expect to win an absolute majority, with the current centre-right coalition coming closest to that goal.

"Apart from the fact that no political, let alone electoral, pact has yet been signed with the Communists, the simulation which gives a potential majority to the left is highly unstable -- a one-percentage-point shift between the ruling coalition candidates and those of the Socialist Party would give an absolute majority to one or the other," the survey said.
Credited with 38 percent of the vote, the Gaullist RPR, more moderate UDF and minor rightist allies would obtain between 234 and 306 seats.
Faced with mounting speculation that President Jacques Chirac could call an early election or order a government reshuffle, his office yesterday denied that either option was on the cards.
Several parliamentarians within the ruling coalition have speculated that holding an early election might secure Chirac a conservative majority for the rest of his seven-year term.
